contributions: Analysis of fundamental limitations of pubsub systems across decoupling, end-to-end guarantees, and scalability
Proposal of an alternative model that unbundles pubsub into an explicit storage abstraction and a watch API
Demonstration that the watch model addresses challenges in replication, cache invalidation, event ingestion, and work queueing with improved end-to-end correctness
Presentation of a watch API with progress and resync signals for recovering lagging consumers and serving snapshot-consistent views
limitations: The paper does not provide quantitative performance benchmarks comparing pubsub vs. the watch model
The Snappy implementation is noted as 'not yet published'
The model assumes a source of truth with monotonic transaction versions (e.g., TrueTime, TSO, gtid), which may not be available in all systems
The paper is truncated before Section 5 (future research areas) and appears to be incomplete
Admitting that resync events may require reading from replicas, potentially introducing staleness
methods: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of pubsub limitations across four use cases (event ingestion/fanout, replication across stores, cache invalidation, and work queueing) and proposes an alternative architectural model. The authors describe a watch API with three callback types (onEvent, onProgress, onResync) and an Ingester interface for distributed change events organized by key and transaction version. Examples are drawn from existing systems including Spanner Change Data Streams, Kubernetes API server with etcd, and a custom implementation called Snappy for MySQL/TiDB.
results: The watch model allows caches and storage replicas to serve snapshot-consistent queries even when dynamically sharded, using progress events scoped to key ranges. Knowledge regions (key range + version window) are immutable, enabling dynamic replication and repartitioning without compromising consistency. The authors show pubsub consumer group mechanisms cannot support independent dynamic sharding of consumers. In cache invalidation, pubsub can miss invalidations during dynamic key range handoffs between pods. For replication, serial approaches lack scalability while concurrent approaches risk snapshot consistency violations (e.g., reordered inserts/deletes can resurrect deleted rows). Some practitioners resort to fallback strategies like periodic full snapshot restores or TTL-based cache expiration.
tldr: Pubsub systems bundle messaging and hard-state storage, which undermines decoupling, violates the end-to-end principle, and causes correctness issues; the authors propose unbundling pubsub into an explicit durable store and a watch-based notification system.
